meta.titre: Group I elements: the alkali metals and their reactivity trend

sections.contenu_markdown: In many Cameroonian villages, soap makers boil palm oil with the ash of burnt plantain peels. That ash is rich in potassium compounds, which make the mixture strongly alkaline and turn the oil into soap. In a Douala market, the salt you buy for 100 FCFA is a compound of sodium, a close relative of potassium. The metals of Group I behave in a very regular way, so once you know the pattern you can predict how any of them reacts. That is why the GCE O/L paper keeps asking about their electronic structure, their reactions with water and their position on the Periodic Table.

items: An atom has protons and neutrons in its nucleus, and electrons in shells around it.
The first shell holds 2 electrons and the second shell holds 8 electrons.
Elements in the same vertical column of the Periodic Table form a group.
A metal is a shiny element that conducts electricity and heat.

sections.titre: Group I: the alkali metals and their trend in reactivity
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Group I** contains lithium (Li), sodium (Na) and potassium (K), followed by rubidium and caesium. They are called the **alkali metals** because they react with water to give alkaline solutions.

**Electronic structure.** Every Group I atom has **one electron in its outer shell**, and that is why the elements sit in Group I. Lithium is 2,1; sodium is 2,8,1; potassium is 2,8,8,1. Each atom loses its single outer electron to form a positive ion with charge 1+, for example $\mathrm{Na \rightarrow Na^{+} + e^{-}}$. The ion then has the stable electronic structure of a noble gas.

**Physical properties.** The metals are soft enough to be cut with a knife, shiny when freshly cut, and have low melting points and low densities. Lithium, sodium and potassium **float on water**. They conduct electricity. Because they react with air and water, they are stored under **oil** (paraffin oil).

**Reaction with water.** The metal floats, melts, and gives off hydrogen. The solution formed is alkaline (it turns red litmus blue and universal indicator purple).

| Metal | What you see with cold water |
|---|---|
| Lithium | Floats and fizzes steadily, slowly disappears |
| Sodium | Melts into a ball, moves quickly over the surface, fizzes |
| Potassium | Melts, reacts violently, hydrogen burns with a lilac flame |

$\mathrm{2Na + 2H_{2}O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_{2}}$

**The trend.** Reactivity **increases down the group**. Going down, atoms have more shells, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus and is shielded by the inner electrons. It is held less strongly, so it is lost more easily.

**Compounds.** Group I compounds are white, ionic solids that dissolve in water. Their hydroxides are strong alkalis.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked how Group I metals burn or form salts
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Group I metals tarnish in air and burn when heated, forming white oxides:

$\mathrm{4Na + O_{2} \rightarrow 2Na_{2}O}$

$\mathrm{4Li + O_{2} \rightarrow 2Li_{2}O}$

They burn in chlorine to make white, ionic chlorides:

$\mathrm{2Na + Cl_{2} \rightarrow 2NaCl}$

The reactions get more vigorous from lithium to potassium. In each compound the metal is present as a 1+ ion, so there is one chloride ion for each metal ion in the chloride (for example $\mathrm{KCl}$).

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a salt must be identified from its flame colour
variantes.contenu_markdown:
To do a flame test, dip a clean nichrome or platinum wire in concentrated hydrochloric acid, then into the solid or solution, and hold it in the edge of a non-luminous Bunsen flame. The colour identifies the metal ion.

| Metal ion | Flame colour |
|---|---|
| Lithium, $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ | Red |
| Sodium, $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ | Yellow (golden-yellow) |
| Potassium, $\mathrm{K^{+}}$ | Lilac |

Sodium gives a strong yellow that hides weaker colours, so a trace of sodium can mask potassium.

sections.enonce_markdown: A student in a school laboratory in Buea drops a small piece of potassium of mass 0.78 g into a large trough of water that contains a few drops of universal indicator. (a) Describe two observations on the metal and the colour change of the indicator. (b) Write a balanced equation. (c) Calculate the volume of hydrogen formed at room temperature and pressure. (d) The solution is made up to 250 cm$^3$. Calculate the concentration of the potassium hydroxide in mol/dm$^3$. ($A_r$: K = 39; 1 mole of gas occupies 24 dm$^3$.)

etapes.justification: Potassium is very reactive, so the reaction is violent.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The metal floats, melts into a ball, moves rapidly and fizzes, and the hydrogen burns with a lilac flame. The indicator turns **purple** because an alkali forms.

etapes.justification: The products are potassium hydroxide and hydrogen.

etapes.action: Use the 2 : 1 ratio and the molar volume.
etapes.justification: The equation shows 2 mol K gives 1 mol $\mathrm{H_2}$.

etapes.action: Find the concentration of the alkali.
etapes.justification: 2 mol K gives 2 mol KOH, so $n(\mathrm{KOH}) = 0.020$ mol in 0.250 dm$^3$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Hydrogen volume = **240 cm$^3$** and the potassium hydroxide solution has a concentration of **0.080 mol/dm$^3$**.

items.erreur_markdown: Group I metals are hard and dense like iron, so they sink in water.
items.pourquoi_faux: Alkali metals are soft and have low density. Lithium, sodium and potassium are less dense than water.
items.correction_markdown: They are soft enough to cut with a knife and they **float** on water.

items.erreur_markdown: Reactivity decreases down Group I because the atoms get bigger.
items.pourquoi_faux: The bigger atom has its outer electron further from the nucleus and more shielded, so the electron is lost more easily.
items.correction_markdown: Reactivity **increases** down the group: potassium reacts more violently than sodium.

items.erreur_markdown: Sodium + water gives sodium oxide: $\mathrm{2Na + H_{2}O \rightarrow Na_{2}O + H_{2}}$
items.pourquoi_faux: Although the equation is balanced, the product is wrong. With water, a Group I metal makes the hydroxide, which dissolves to give an alkaline solution.

items.erreur_markdown: The solution formed is acidic because hydrogen is produced.
items.pourquoi_faux: Hydrogen is a gas that escapes. The solution contains hydroxide ions, so it is alkaline.
items.correction_markdown: The solution turns red litmus blue and universal indicator purple.

items.erreur_markdown: Sodium is kept under water to stop it burning in air.
items.pourquoi_faux: Sodium reacts with water. It must be kept away from both water and air.
items.correction_markdown: Store Group I metals under paraffin oil.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Write the electronic configurations of a sodium atom (atomic number 11) and a potassium atom (atomic number 19). (b) State what the two configurations have in common. (c) Give the formula of the ion each atom forms and the flame colour of each metal.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Sodium: **2,8,1**. Potassium: **2,8,8,1**. (b) Each has **one electron in its outer shell**, so both are in Group I. (c) Each atom loses its outer electron: $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ (flame **yellow**) and $\mathrm{K^{+}}$ (flame **lilac**).

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Write a balanced equation for sodium burning in chlorine and name the product. (b) Write a balanced equation for lithium burning in oxygen. (c) A piece of lithium is placed in water. State two observations and how you would show that the solution is alkaline.
items.solution_markdown: (a) $\mathrm{2Na + Cl_{2} \rightarrow 2NaCl}$, the product is **sodium chloride**. (b) $\mathrm{4Li + O_{2} \rightarrow 2Li_{2}O}$ (c) The lithium floats and fizzes steadily as hydrogen is given off, and it slowly disappears. Add a few drops of universal indicator, which turns **purple** (or red litmus paper turns blue), so the solution is alkaline.

items.enonce_markdown: A piece of sodium of mass 0.69 g reacts completely with water and the solution is made up to 500 cm$^3$. ($A_r$: Na = 23; O = 16; H = 1; 1 mole of gas = 24 dm$^3$.) (a) Write the balanced equation. (b) Calculate the volume of hydrogen formed. (c) Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide formed. (d) Calculate the mass of sodium hydroxide in the solution.

items_markdown: Group I metals (Li, Na, K) have **one outer electron** and form **1+ ions**.
They are soft, shiny when cut, of low density, and are stored under oil.
With water they give hydrogen and an **alkaline** hydroxide: $\mathrm{2Na + 2H_{2}O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_{2}}$
Reactivity **increases down the group** because the outer electron is further away and more shielded.
Flame colours: Li red, Na yellow, K lilac.
